questions.question: Design a notification service that sends email, SMS, and push notifications.
questions.title: Design a Notification Service (Email, SMS, Push)
questions.direct_answer: Decouple notification dispatch from business logic via a **Kafka event bus**. A **Notification Orchestrator** consumes domain events, looks up **user preferences and templates**, and emits **per-channel messages** to dedicated worker pools (Email, SMS, Push). Each worker calls its provider (SendGrid, Twilio, FCM/APNS) with **retry-with-exponential-backoff**, **provider-side rate limiting**, **DLQ** for poison messages, and **idempotency keys** to prevent duplicates. A **delivery-status pipeline** ingests provider webhooks back into the system for tracking and analytics.

interviewer_intent.testing: Event-driven decoupling, multi-channel orchestration, retry/failure semantics, idempotency at scale, and template/preference management.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Calling SendGrid/Twilio directly from the producing service, or treating retries naively (no exponential backoff, no DLQ, no idempotency).
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Discuss user preferences and quiet hours, template versioning, deduplication via idempotency keys, provider failover, and how delivery status loops back through provider webhooks.

sections.title: Framing the Problem and What Makes This Hard
sections.content:
A notification service looks like a thin wrapper around SendGrid/Twilio/FCM. The complexity hides in operational reality:

- **Many producers, many channels** — every product team wants to send notifications. If each calls SendGrid directly, you have N×M coupling, no central preference enforcement, and no consistent retry behavior.
- **Provider failures are normal** — SMS providers throttle, FCM rate-limits, SendGrid has bad regions. Retries with exponential backoff and DLQ are the floor, not nice-to-haves.
- **Duplicates are catastrophic** — "your password was reset" sent twice causes support tickets. Idempotency must be first-class.
- **Preferences and quiet hours** — GDPR/CAN-SPAM compliance, user opt-out, time-zone-aware quiet hours. Centralized in the notification service or every team reimplements (badly).
- **Templates evolve faster than code** — marketing wants to A/B-test subject lines without a deploy. Templates need a separate lifecycle.
- **Rate limits are global per provider** — Twilio caps your account at N msgs/sec across all your services. The notification service is the natural enforcement point.
- **Delivery confirmation is async and out-of-order** — webhooks arrive seconds to hours later; we need to correlate them back to the original send.

The core architectural decision: **make the notification service the single dispatch path** so preferences, retries, rate limits, idempotency, and observability are enforced once, not N times.

sections.title: Clarifying Questions I'd Ask First
sections.content:
**Functional**
- Which channels are in scope: **email, SMS, mobile push (iOS+Android), web push, in-app, voice**?
- **Template management** — self-serve via UI for marketing, or always code-deployed?
- **Multi-language / localization** required?
- **User preferences** — per-channel, per-category, both?
- **Scheduled / delayed notifications** (e.g., "send 3 days after signup")?
- **Bulk campaigns** (1M users at once) vs **transactional** (one per event)?
- **Delivery status tracking** required — dashboards for marketing?

**Non-functional**
- **Volume per channel** — typically email is highest, SMS lowest (cost).
- **Latency budget** — transactional ("OTP code") needs sub-second; marketing campaigns can be minutes.
- **Provider redundancy** — do we need failover between providers (SendGrid → Mailgun)?
- **Compliance** — GDPR, CAN-SPAM, TCPA — affects opt-out enforcement and audit trail.
- **Multi-tenancy** — internal tool only, or sold as a platform to external customers?

sections.title: Assumptions I'm Locking In
sections.content:
- **3 channels in scope**: email, SMS, mobile push.
- **100M users**, **~10M notifications/day** (mixed: 70% email, 20% push, 10% SMS) plus **occasional 50M-recipient campaigns**.
- **Latency**: transactional notifications dispatched within **5 seconds p99**; marketing campaigns may take minutes.
- **One primary provider per channel** with **at least one failover** configured but not auto-promoted (manual switch on outage).
- **Templates managed in a separate Template Service** with versioning and A/B variants.
- **User preferences per channel + per category** (e.g., user can opt out of "marketing" emails but keep "transactional").
- **Idempotency** — every notification request carries an `idempotency_key` from the producer; duplicates within 24 hours are silently dropped.
- **Quiet hours** respected per user time zone for non-urgent categories.

sections.title: Back-of-Envelope Capacity Estimate
sections.content:
**Steady state**

- 10M notifications/day ÷ 86,400 ≈ **~115/sec average**.
- Peak (e.g., morning bulk send window): **~2,000/sec**.
- Per-channel split: **~1,400 email/sec, ~400 push/sec, ~200 SMS/sec at peak**.

**Campaign burst**

- 50M-recipient campaign: at sustained 5,000/sec, takes ~3 hours. Or with 20,000/sec burst across all workers, ~40 minutes.
- Provider rate limits often gate this, not us — SendGrid lets you burst to ~10K msgs/sec with a paid tier.

**Storage**

- Notification record per send: ~1 KB (id, user_id, channel, template, status, timestamps).
- 10M/day × 1 KB = **10 GB/day** → ~3.6 TB/year. Comfortable in PostgreSQL with monthly partitioning, or push to S3 + Athena for older data.

**Provider rate limits (typical paid tier)**

- SendGrid: ~10,000/sec
- Twilio SMS: ~100/sec per long code, ~500/sec per short code
- FCM: ~36,000/min per app
- APNS: ~1,000/sec per HTTP/2 connection

**Conclusion:** SMS is the bottleneck and the cost driver. Architecture must let us throttle per-channel independently and queue for hours if needed without losing messages.

sections.title: API Contract
sections.content:
Producers call a single REST endpoint (or publish to a Kafka topic) with channel-agnostic intent:

```http
POST /api/v1/notifications
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "idempotency_key": "order-12345-confirmation",
  "user_id": "u_99",
  "category": "transactional",            // or "marketing", "alert"
  "template_id": "order_shipped_v3",
  "template_data": {
    "order_id": "12345",
    "tracking_url": "https://..."
  },
  "channels": ["email", "push"],          // optional; defaults to user prefs
  "send_at": null                          // optional ISO timestamp for scheduled
}

202 Accepted
{
  "notification_id": "ntf_7Z3kY8",
  "status": "queued"
}
```

Status query and webhook for delivery callbacks:

```http
GET /api/v1/notifications/{id}

200 OK
{
  "notification_id": "ntf_7Z3kY8",
  "status": "delivered",                   // queued | sent | delivered | failed | bounced
  "channels": [
    {"channel":"email",  "status":"delivered", "provider":"sendgrid", "delivered_at":"..."},
    {"channel":"push",   "status":"sent",      "provider":"fcm"}
  ]
}
```

Provider webhooks are received on dedicated endpoints — each provider has its own format:

```http
POST /webhooks/sendgrid    POST /webhooks/twilio    POST /webhooks/fcm
```

sections.title: Data Model
sections.content:
**Core tables (PostgreSQL):**

**`notifications`** — the request record:

| Column | Type |
|---|---|
| `notification_id` | UUID PK |
| `idempotency_key` | TEXT UNIQUE |
| `user_id` | BIGINT |
| `category` | enum(transactional, marketing, alert) |
| `template_id` | TEXT |
| `template_data` | JSONB |
| `requested_channels` | TEXT[] |
| `status` | enum(queued, dispatching, completed, failed) |
| `created_at` | TIMESTAMPTZ |
| `send_at` | TIMESTAMPTZ NULL |

**`channel_dispatches`** — one row per channel per notification:

| Column | Type |
|---|---|
| `dispatch_id` | UUID PK |
| `notification_id` | UUID FK |
| `channel` | enum(email, sms, push) |
| `provider` | TEXT |
| `provider_message_id` | TEXT |
| `status` | enum(pending, sent, delivered, failed, bounced) |
| `attempt_count` | INT |
| `next_attempt_at` | TIMESTAMPTZ |
| `last_error` | TEXT |

**`user_preferences`** — per-user opt-in/out matrix:

| Column | Type |
|---|---|
| `user_id` | BIGINT PK |
| `category` | TEXT PK |
| `channel` | TEXT PK |
| `enabled` | BOOLEAN |
| `quiet_hours_start` | TIME |
| `quiet_hours_end` | TIME |
| `time_zone` | TEXT |

**`templates`** (in Template Service — separate store, versioned):

| Column | Type |
|---|---|
| `template_id` | TEXT PK |
| `version` | INT PK |
| `channel` | enum |
| `locale` | TEXT |
| `subject` | TEXT (email only) |
| `body` | TEXT (Mustache/Handlebars) |
| `is_active` | BOOLEAN |

Relationships:

```mermaid
erDiagram
    USERS ||--o{ NOTIFICATIONS : receives
    USERS ||--o{ USER_PREFERENCES : configures
    NOTIFICATIONS ||--|{ CHANNEL_DISPATCHES : fanned_into
    TEMPLATES ||--o{ NOTIFICATIONS : rendered_from
    NOTIFICATIONS {
        uuid notification_id PK
        text idempotency_key UK
        bigint user_id FK
        text template_id
        enum status
    }
    CHANNEL_DISPATCHES {
        uuid dispatch_id PK
        uuid notification_id FK
        enum channel
        text provider_message_id
        enum status
        int attempt_count
    }
    USER_PREFERENCES {
        bigint user_id FK
        text category
        enum channel
        bool enabled
    }
    TEMPLATES {
        text template_id PK
        int version PK
        enum channel
        text body
    }
```

sections.title: Notification Orchestrator — The Core Logic
sections.content:
The Orchestrator turns a single "send notification" intent into one or more per-channel dispatches. Pipeline:

1. **Idempotency dedup** — if `idempotency_key` already exists with status not-failed in last 24 hours, drop and return existing notification_id.
2. **Fetch user preferences** for `(user_id, category)` — list of enabled channels.
3. **Intersect requested channels with enabled channels** — if user opted out of marketing emails, no email is sent.
4. **Quiet-hours check** — for non-transactional categories, if current time in user's TZ is in quiet window, schedule for end of window.
5. **Template resolution** — fetch the active version of `template_id` for the channel and locale; render with `template_data`.
6. **Persist `channel_dispatches` rows** with `status=pending`.
7. **Publish to per-channel topic**.

Why this lives in one orchestrator (not in workers): centralized preference enforcement and quiet-hours logic means we can add new channels or new categories without touching N worker codebases.

**Transactional vs marketing distinction** — transactional notifications ("OTP", "order shipped") **bypass quiet hours and ignore opt-out** (legally required and user-expected). Marketing notifications respect both.

sections.title: Per-Channel Workers, Retries, and Rate Limiting
sections.content:
Each channel has a dedicated worker pool. The shape of the worker is similar; the differences are in the provider client and rate limits.

**Worker loop:**

1. Consume from `dispatch.{channel}` topic
2. Acquire a token from the **per-provider rate limiter** (Redis token bucket, shared across worker instances)
3. Call provider HTTP API with idempotency header
4. On 2xx → update `dispatch.status = sent`, record `provider_message_id`
5. On 4xx (bad recipient, invalid template) → mark `failed`, do not retry
6. On 5xx or timeout → schedule retry with exponential backoff (1s, 4s, 16s, 1m, 5m, 30m)
7. After 6 retries → send to DLQ for manual inspection

**Rate limiting per provider** — each worker instance shares a Redis-backed token bucket keyed by provider:

- `rate:sendgrid` — capacity 10000, refill 10000/sec
- `rate:twilio:short_code_X` — capacity 500, refill 500/sec
- `rate:fcm:app_id` — capacity 600, refill 600/sec

**Provider failover** — if SendGrid returns sustained 5xx (circuit breaker trips), the email worker switches to Mailgun for new messages. Provider config is externalized; no deploy needed.

**Idempotency at the provider** — SendGrid and Twilio both accept idempotency keys; we send `dispatch_id` so a retry doesn't double-send even if the previous attempt actually succeeded but the response was lost.

sections.title: LLD — Class Design of the Dispatch Pipeline
Idempotency, Templates, and Preferences — The Three Cross-Cutting Pieces
sections.content:
**Idempotency**

- Producer supplies `idempotency_key` (e.g., `order-12345-confirmation`).
- API checks `notifications.idempotency_key` index; if exists with status not-failed within 24h, return existing `notification_id`.
- If exists with `failed` status, allow re-attempt under the same key.
- TTL of 24 hours — longer encourages duplicate suppression bugs hiding for too long.

**Templates**

- Stored in a separate **Template Service** with versioning.
- Template ID + version + channel + locale uniquely identifies a template body.
- A new version is uploaded; tested via shadow traffic; promoted to `is_active=true`.
- Renderer uses Mustache or Handlebars — logic-less templates so non-engineers can edit.
- Rendered output cached for 5 minutes per (template_id, version, hash-of-data) — same notification repeated to many users hits cache.

**Preferences**

- Default opt-in for transactional, opt-out for marketing.
- Stored as one row per (user, category, channel) tuple — sparse representation, only diffs from defaults.
- Cache aggressively in Redis (TTL 5 min) — every send hits this lookup.
- Preferences UI is a separate product; the notification service exposes a read API.

sections.title: Failure Modes and Resilience
sections.content:
**Provider outage (SendGrid down)**

- 5xx responses trigger circuit breaker.
- Email worker switches to Mailgun via config flip (no deploy).
- In-flight messages retry with backoff; queue drains as soon as recovery happens.

**Database unavailable**

- API returns 503 with `Retry-After`.
- Kafka topic is the durable record; orchestrator can replay on recovery.
- DB writes for `channel_dispatches` are best-effort — if DB is down briefly, the worker still attempts the send and updates status when DB recovers.

**Worker crash mid-send**

- Kafka offset hasn't been committed — another worker picks up the message.
- Provider idempotency header (`Idempotency-Key: dispatch_id`) prevents double-send if previous attempt actually reached the provider.

**Webhook delivery loss**

- Provider may retry webhooks for hours, but some get lost.
- Reconciliation job runs daily: query provider's API for status of dispatches stuck in `sent` for > 1 hour and update.

**DLQ growth**

- DLQ is monitored; alerts fire on > 100 messages.
- Manual inspection identifies bug, fix is deployed, messages replayed via DLQ replayer tool.

**Bulk campaign bursts**

- Producer for marketing campaigns emits at controlled rate (5,000/sec sustained).
- Per-channel rate limiters smooth further.
- Transactional and marketing share infrastructure but use **separate Kafka topics with priority consumer ratios** — transactional gets 80% of worker capacity, marketing gets 20% during high-volume periods.

sections.title: Observability and Security
sections.content:
**Metrics per channel**

- `notifications.requested.total{category, channel}`
- `notifications.sent.total{provider, status}`
- `notifications.delivery.latency` (queued → sent)
- `notifications.delivery.success_rate{provider}` — alert below 95%
- `kafka.lag{topic}` — backpressure indicator
- `dlq.depth` — alert above threshold
- `provider.api.latency{provider}` and `provider.api.errors{provider, code}`

**Per-notification trace**

- Distributed trace ID propagated from producer through orchestrator into provider call.
- Each `notification_id` queryable in dashboard with full lifecycle: requested → dispatched → sent → delivered.

**Security**

- **Provider credentials in secret manager** (Vault/AWS Secrets Manager), rotated quarterly.
- **Webhook signature verification** — each provider signs webhook payloads (HMAC); reject unsigned/invalid.
- **PII handling** — template data may contain emails, phone numbers, names. Logs scrub PII; long-term storage encrypted at rest.
- **Per-tenant rate limits** if multi-tenant — prevent one team's bug from exhausting our SendGrid quota.
- **Compliance audit log** — every send recorded with category, opt-in proof timestamp, IP. Required for GDPR/CAN-SPAM disputes.

sections.title: Trade-offs and What I'd Change at 10× Scale
sections.content:
**At 10× scale (100M notifications/day, 500M-recipient campaigns):**

- **Sharded notification API** by `user_id` hash to spread DB write load.
- **Per-region dispatch infrastructure** — each region calls regional provider endpoints (SendGrid EU, US).
- **Pre-rendered template cache** in CDN-style edge cache for high-volume templates.
- **Replace per-message DB write with batched writes** (1,000 dispatches per insert) for marketing campaigns.

**What I'd reconsider:**

- **Single Kafka cluster vs per-channel clusters** — isolating SMS Kafka from email Kafka means one channel's lag spike doesn't affect others; pays for itself at high volume.
- **Per-user opt-out enforcement at producer vs orchestrator** — if multiple producers exist, opt-out at producer is faster but harder to keep consistent. Centralizing in orchestrator is correctness-first.

**What I rejected and why:**

- **Direct provider calls from each producing service** — N×M coupling, no central preferences, no consistent retries.
- **Synchronous send** — ties producer latency to provider latency; one provider hiccup blocks order confirmation.
- **Single global rate limiter for all providers** — different providers have wildly different limits; lumping them under one budget wastes capacity.
- **Storing rendered email body in the DB** — wastes space and slows queries; render at dispatch time and discard.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Single notification API** with idempotency keys is the entry point — no producer talks to providers directly.
- **Kafka per-channel topics** isolate failure and scaling — SMS outage doesn't block email.
- **Notification Orchestrator** centralizes preference enforcement, quiet hours, template resolution, and fan-out across channels.
- **`ChannelDispatcher` and `ProviderClient` interfaces** make providers swappable and let us A/B-test SendGrid vs Mailgun without code changes.
- **Retry with exponential backoff + DLQ** at every worker; provider idempotency keys prevent duplicates from successful-but-lost responses.
- **Per-provider Redis token-bucket rate limiters** — globally enforce provider quotas across all worker instances.
- **Webhook receiver loops delivery status back into the DB** — single source of truth for delivery analytics; daily reconciliation job catches missed webhooks.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
**Clarifying questions I'd ask first**

- Which channels: email, SMS, push, web push, in-app?
- Self-serve template management for marketing or always code-deployed?
- User preferences — per channel, per category, both?
- Scheduled or delayed notifications?
- Bulk marketing campaigns vs purely transactional?
- Compliance requirements — GDPR, TCPA, CAN-SPAM?

**Assumptions for this design**

Three channels: email, SMS, mobile push. 100 million users, ~10 million notifications a day with 70/20/10 mix, plus occasional 50-million-recipient campaigns. Sub-5-second p99 dispatch for transactional. Idempotency keys from every producer. Quiet hours respected for non-transactional categories.

**Quick capacity check**

- Steady state: ~115 notifications/sec, ~2,000/sec at peak
- Per-channel split at peak: ~1,400 email, ~400 push, ~200 SMS
- Provider rate limits: SendGrid ~10K/sec, Twilio ~500/sec, FCM ~36K/min
- SMS is the cost driver and the bottleneck — design must throttle per-channel independently

**High-level shape**

- Producers POST to a single Notification API or publish to Kafka
- API does idempotency dedup against `notifications.idempotency_key` and writes to a Kafka topic
- Notification Orchestrator consumes, resolves preferences and templates, fans out to per-channel topics
- Per-channel worker pools (Email, SMS, Push) consume their topic, acquire rate-limit tokens from Redis, call providers with idempotency headers
- Webhook receivers ingest provider callbacks (delivered, bounced) and update the dispatch status
- DLQ catches poison messages after retry exhaustion

**Why per-channel queues, not one big queue**

If SMS provider goes down, email shouldn't be blocked. Per-channel topics give independent scaling, independent rate limits, independent failure domains. Same reasoning for per-channel worker pools.

**The Orchestrator pipeline — step by step**

- Idempotency dedup on `idempotency_key`
- Look up user preferences for `(user_id, category)` — list of enabled channels
- Intersect requested channels with enabled channels
- Quiet-hours check for non-transactional categories — schedule for later if needed
- Resolve template (template_id, version, channel, locale), render with template_data
- Persist `channel_dispatches` rows with status=pending
- Publish to per-channel Kafka topic

**Transactional vs marketing**

- Transactional (OTP, order shipped) bypasses quiet hours and ignores marketing opt-out — user-expected and often legally required
- Marketing respects both, plus separate rate budgets
- Both share infrastructure but use separate topics with priority consumer ratios so a campaign burst doesn't starve transactional

**Worker loop — retries and rate limits**

- Acquire token from Redis per-provider rate limiter (token bucket)
- Call provider with idempotency header (so retries don't double-send if prior response was lost)
- 2xx: mark sent, store provider_message_id
- 4xx (bad recipient): mark failed, no retry
- 5xx or timeout: schedule retry with exponential backoff (1s, 4s, 16s, 1m, 5m, 30m)
- After 6 retries: DLQ
- Provider failover: circuit breaker on sustained 5xx switches to alternate provider via config flip

**Data model**

- `notifications` table: the request, with idempotency_key UNIQUE
- `channel_dispatches` table: one row per channel per notification, tracks status and attempts
- `user_preferences` table: per-user, per-category, per-channel enable/disable plus quiet hours
- Templates in a separate Template Service with versioning — marketing changes templates without code deploy

**LLD — clean abstractions**

- `ChannelDispatcher` interface per channel — each has its own policy
- `ProviderClient` interface inside each dispatcher — SendGrid and Mailgun are interchangeable
- `RateLimiter` and `RetryScheduler` as separate collaborators — testable in isolation
- `IdempotencyChecker` at the controller boundary — duplicates never enter the pipeline

**Failure handling**

- Provider outage: circuit breaker → failover to alternate provider
- DB down briefly: Kafka is durable record; orchestrator replays on recovery
- Worker crash mid-send: another worker picks up; provider idempotency header prevents double-send
- Webhook loss: daily reconciliation job queries provider APIs for stuck-in-sent dispatches
- Bulk campaign burst: producer-side rate limiting plus per-channel limits prevent SendGrid quota exhaustion

**Production extras**

- Provider credentials in secret manager, rotated
- Webhook signature verification (HMAC) on every callback
- PII scrubbed from logs; long-term storage encrypted
- Compliance audit log: every send with category, opt-in proof, IP
- Distributed tracing across producer → orchestrator → provider

**At 10× scale**

- Sharded notification API by user_id hash
- Per-region dispatch infrastructure with regional provider endpoints
- Pre-rendered template cache for high-volume templates
- Batched DB writes for marketing campaigns

**Recommendation**

**A single notification API with idempotency keys, Kafka per-channel topics, a Notification Orchestrator that centralizes preferences and templates, per-channel worker pools with provider abstraction and Redis-backed rate limiters, exponential-backoff retries with DLQ, and a webhook receiver that loops delivery status back into the DB** — essentially the architecture Twilio's own customers and most large product companies run.

followup_questions: How would you implement webhook delivery for external customers — the inverse problem where you're the provider notifying their endpoints?
How do you handle a marketing campaign of 100M recipients without overwhelming SendGrid or starving transactional traffic?
What changes if you need strict ordering of notifications per user (e.g., "order placed" before "order shipped")?
How would you build A/B testing for templates without slowing down the dispatch path?

beats.text: A notification service looks like a thin wrapper around SendGrid/Twilio/FCM. The complexity hides in operational reality: Many producers, many channels — every product team wants to send notifications. If each calls SendGrid directly, you have N×M coupling, no central preference enforcement, and no consistent retry behavior. Provider failures are normal — SMS providers throttle, FCM rate-limits, SendGrid has bad regions. Retries with exponential backoff and DLQ are the floor, not nice-to-haves. Duplicates are catastrophic — "your password was reset" sent twice causes support tickets. Idempotency must be first-class. Preferences and quiet hours — GDPR/CAN-SPAM compliance, user opt-out, time-zone-aware quiet hours. Centralized in the notification service or every team reimplements (badly). Templates evolve faster than code — marketing wants to A/B-test.

Calling SendGrid/Twilio directly from the producing service, or treating retries naively (no exponential backoff, no DLQ, no idempotency).

Single notification API with idempotency keys is the entry point — no producer talks to providers directly. Kafka per-channel topics isolate failure and scaling — SMS outage doesn't block email. Notification Orchestrator centralizes preference enforcement, quiet hours, template resolution, and fan-out across channels. ChannelDispatcher and ProviderClient interfaces make providers swappable and let us A/B-test SendGrid vs Mailgun without code changes. Retry with exponential backoff + DLQ at every worker; provider idempotency keys prevent duplicates from successful-but-lost responses. Per-provider Redis token-bucket rate limiters — globally enforce.
